title: I'm working on a card game that is generated in real-time
author: interestingsystems
selftext:
Thronedream is a solo-play narrative card game where all the content is generated in real-time, based on the setting and player character that you choose.

So far, the majority of AI-native games are text adventures, text RPGs, or character-focused games that use AI for NPC dialogue. With Thronedream I am exploring new ground in this space - I don't know if this is the first card game using AI (I've seen a couple of "card battlers" which use AI in more limited ways), but I think it is the first where all the content is dynamically generated.

The core rules of the card game are human designed (and fixed), while AI generates the cards and narrative in real-time:

* Instead of a deckbuilding / card draw mechanic, the player selects a card from a draft of 3 dynamically generated cards every turn
* Each game has a 3-act narrative structure, with a player objective for each act selected by the AI to complement the story
* Threat cards, i.e. the obstacles faced by the player character, are dynamically generated as part of the narrative
* At regular intervals, the player chooses how the story continues from two possible events (this can be scaled back or turned off, based on playstyle and cost preferences).

I've put together a longer [video](https://youtu.be/IpvhByArV-w) where I play through a game as a patrician in an ancient Rome ruled by vampires, so you can see what it is like and judge for yourself whether it works. There's also a [website](https://www.thronedream.com/). If this sounds like something you'd be interested in playing, there is a [waitlist](https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSch0U1hnS39arHOdf-M9EZf2K0dCNtidic0I54F2CRvvRC-fQ/viewform?usp=header) you can sign up to, I will be opening up early access to a first small batch of players soon.

This is pretty experimental territory, so I'm genuinely curious what developers here think of this approach. Happy to dive into any technical details or design decisions if anyone wants to discuss - I've learned a lot building this and would love to hear from others working in this space.

comments.author: PikachuDash
comments.body: How do you deal with the game balance? I would reckon that the AI will create some wildly overpowered, some wildly underpowered cards.

replies.author: interestingsystems
replies.body: Most of the mechanical side is (currently) procedurally generated, not using an LLM. When it comes to cards specifically, the card is procedurally generated, and then themed by generative AI to fit the world and the narrative. In some other areas I use an LLM to pick in-game effects, but in that case its picking from a pre-balanced set of options.

comments.author: AxiosXiphos
comments.body: Very interesting concept. Content being generated live in games in something we are only just starting to see come to fruition.

replies.author: interestingsystems
replies.body: Thank you. It's an exciting new frontier.

replies.author: AxiosXiphos
replies.body: I joined the wait list, look forward to hearing more about it.

comments.author: FailedGradAdmissions
comments.body:
Genuinely curious, how do you plan to monetize it. Most Indie Games in this category (solo narrative card games) are priced as a one time $10-20 purchase.

You surely can’t do that right as AI image gen is expensive, right? So subscription or credit based? But that would be a tough sell.

replies.author: interestingsystems
replies.body:
That's the big question. Image generation is expensive. Text generation is even more expensive - the game has less text to read than a game like AI Dungeon (of course), but the token usage under the hood is actually surprisingly high because of all the design work the AI is doing.

I'm betting that the cost of inference will at some point go down. Until then, I'm hoping there will be a small audience that is willing to pay the generation costs and that will make this project sustainable for me personally. My initial implementation is credit based, but subscription is a natural next step.

replies.author: TiagoDev
replies.body: A combination of local and server models could offset the costs. Simpler bits locally, complex ones in the server?

replies.author: interestingsystems
replies.body: At some point, hopefully yes! Right now, local models with any decent intelligence are too slow on typical consumer hardware to apply them to this kind of experience. They're good for roleplay, but this kind of game might not become viable in a serious way until the hardware catches up.

replies.author: SlowMoneyBall
replies.body: How do you feel about the end points that share data for training with the LLM providers? (If disclosed properly to the end user). Seems like the best way to keep the text generation piece costs low.

replies.author: interestingsystems
replies.body:
I know OpenRouter (which I use) has free end points that typically share data, but those free end points come with prohibitive rate limits, which means you cannot realistically build a service on top of them anyway. Otherwise, I'm not aware of any end points that provide cheaper inference costs for sharing data for training with the LLM provider. 

I'd have no issue with it in principle, assuming it was properly disclosed (and possibly allowing opt-out).

replies.author: icekiller333
replies.body:
Have you considered a way to save images and story that is generated by each user and then pulling from that database later when there are requests for the same information. 

Like if 1000 people all want a dancing clown vampire, is it really worth the resources to generate 1000 of those, or would pulling from the database be worthwhile. Maybe each request for something thats already in the database would have a % chance of generating something new verse pulling, so you still have new content being generated but at a reduced volume.

replies.author: interestingsystems
replies.body:
That is a possibility.

There's basically a range of ways to design this game - consider a scale where at one end we have normal fixed card games, and on the other end we have a card game that is so adaptable to what the player wants and does, that the game plays out completely uniquely to that player. If we design for somewhere in the middle of that scale, than we would have say 100-1000 possible settings, and once the player picks one they get served the cards of that setting.

So far I've opted instead to go for the far end of the scale because what attracts me is the idea of a game which really adapts to you and what happens. Where picking a particular card in a draft can affect the narrative, and then the narrative affects how the world changes, and that affects what cards you draw. I'm not saying that full vision is there yet, but what I already have is meaningfully in that direction, and will continue to improve as AI models become better. 

For example, in the linked playthrough of the ancient Roman vampires, you'll see that because I played a gladiator character, that pulled in more cards that had a gladiator theme, and because I played an architect character, that pulled in more related cards (I got quite a few military units that were engineers or fortification assault, for example). 

Similarly, the threat cards tell a story. At one point, the threat card played was "Echoes of Sacrilege", themed as "Lucius's desecration of the Curia Occulta \[an earlier event in the narrative\] unleashed lingering blood wraiths that now haunt the sacred spaces". And then on the next turn, the threat card was that the humans that work in those sacred spaces (specifically two locations I had played) had been driven mad by the blood wraiths, and needed to be put down. There's no way you would get that kind of natural flow of story with pre-defined cards.

And the overarching narrative would likely have to be fairly static or at least tightly constrained. It certainly couldn't interact specifically with cards you draw and play (in the "Full" story mode, not shown in the video, character cards you draw feature prominently in the story that plays out).

All that said, I have considered making both versions of the game and letting the player switch between them, but of course there's a lot of additional implementation complexity there.

replies.author: interestingsystems
replies.body: Oh, I do intend to use this strategy for music btw. I haven't added music into the game yet, but I do pretty much intend to reuse music between players, and just sustain the cost of that myself.

replies.author: ezoterik
replies.body:
I like the idea and the cards are looking really good too.

I've seen a few people create AI card games here on Reddit. I've also built a simple card game, but it doesn't use AI. I've explored AI generated content in a few apps, but I fear it isn't quite there yet. 

For example, in one app I try to generate novels using a fixed procedure and while the generated text is reasonable and in some ways human-like, but the coherency of the story is noticeable imperfect.

I find LLMs aren't particularly great with randomness, at least when it comes to text. I did a mini-research project to "prove" that. Despite the seeming non-determinism of LLMs, the amount of randomness is limited.

For a game, it might be ok though. I've been slowly working on an AI-powered D&D game, which generates text in response to user prompts. I did consider coding it in such a way that AI could generate art on the fly, but I also feared the costs and the general slowness.

It is an interesting engineer problem. I wonder if you can use/abuse a RAG system where a request performs a semantic search over previously generated cards and use that one instead of regenerating. Idk, just a thought.

replies.author: interestingsystems
replies.body:
Thank you!

Yeah LLMs aren't particularly great with randomness, you kind of have to inject it externally. That's one of the advantages of pairing it with procedural generation, because then they're really good at taking a seed idea and running with it.

A RAG system would make sense as the way to match previously generated cards if you were going for the more static settings design.

comments.author: HelfenMich
comments.body: Really cool stuff! Can you talk about what AI tools you're using outside of the image generation? Like, what does your development workflow look like?

replies.author: interestingsystems
replies.body:
I'm not really using any third party AI tooling - I've built everything myself on top of raw API calls. There are some tools I would like to use, top of my list being DSPy, but I'm working in a C# stack and AFAIK there is no C# port of DSPy yet. Otherwise I've built a basic set of tools to make it easier to examine and evaluate LLM traces quickly. I am interested myself in third party tooling here, but I haven't particularly found anything worth investing in yet.  
  
That probably isn't a very useful answer. If you have a more specific question, I can try addressing it better.

replies.author: HelfenMich
replies.body:
Yeah, I was just wondering if you were using anything outside of the API calls. I'm also on a C# stack because it's what I'm used to from the last ~15 years of work.

I'm currently working on Yet Another Text Adventure Game, and I've been using LLMs for project management, architecture/brainstorming, and creative director. I also use it for some coding (mostly boilerplate and third party library calls).

I have a whole workflow developed for running my project in sort of a hybrid-AI agile methodology so I was just curious if you were doing anything similar. It feels like a lot of AI game devs are coming at things from wildly different angles, it's fun to learn how everyone else is accomplishing things.

replies.author: interestingsystems
replies.body:
Ah I see. Same here re C#.  
  
I use LLMs a lot for brainstorming, research, and analysis. But I have struggled to use them for coding. I am using AI code completion extensively, but I've only used agent coding tools (i.e. Claude Code) for tooling. There it's been excellent, and has allowed me to rapidly write little utilities and support tools that would have been very time consuming earlier. Such tools are straightforward enough that I haven't needed to develop any specific workflow.  
  
But when it comes to the core game, there's enough complexity that I don't quite trust the AI to do any significant work on it. In the past I've found that the time required to specify something in detail (when there are a lot of considerations because of project complexity), plus the time required to verify and clean up the resulting code, outweighs any saving from using agent coders. Admittedly my assessment is a few months old now, so I may be out of date.

I'm actually more interested in applying AI at the project management level, but I have not yet found a system that works well. I'd be interested to know what your workflow looks like.

replies.author: HelfenMich
replies.body:
I haven't found a third party system that works for me because well, I'm picky. My workflow, as such, is basically this:

1. Work with architect/brainstorming LLM chat to determine feasibility and the structure of a new feature 
2. Turn that work into an epic. I capture all of the documentation for an Epic and shuttle that off to Google Drive for the future
3. Now, I choose an epic I'd like to work on. For an example, let's say my epic is "character stats/attributes". 
4. I work with my architect LLM to break this down into individual, detailed tasks
5. I take that list of individual tasks to my Project Manager LLM
6. We go through each one and talk about estimates. It's a solo project so who cares about estimates, but... I like them. The PM also uses this info to ask follow-up questions later.
7. The PM generates a CSV file that lays out the tasks
8. I import the CSV into a GitHub Issues board which creates all my individual tasks on the board
9. Now I go task by task and work them. Sometimes I'll tackle it 100% solo (especially config stuff). Most of the time I at least use the GitHub Copilot agent in VS to review the task and give its suggestions, even if I don't always use them. But honestly, more often than not the AI does a good enough job that I only need to make a few edits. I will optionally ask a second, different LLM if I need a second opinion.
10. After I finish an epic, I commit all my changes and report back to my different LLMs for a debrief. PM will debrief about how it went, if it was harder than expected for any reason, etc. Architect debrief will be about what, if anything, I had to change from the original design or direction, any challenges, etc.

I'll usually have a few epics in the backlog at any time, and lots waiting for refinement. That way I can decide at any point in time if I feel like talking about new stuff or just coding things we've already talked about and refined.

I'm aware that I've basically used AI to recreate my own solo version of enterprise software dev, but I just really feel comfortable with the structure it provides. I think this workflow has also led to a pretty successful project thus far because of my existing experience - I know when to push back and tell an AI Coder "nah dude we are not doing it that way", and I already have a LOT of experience talking to architects and project managers. The more I communicate with my AI "team members" like I do with my actual team at work, the more successful I've been with getting good work built.

replies.author: interestingsystems
replies.body: I get it. A large part of working out a good solution is talking about it with different parties, particularly if they focus on a particular aspect and can challenge your assumptions in that area. I haven't used anything like this - I have discussed specific problems that I was stuck on with LLMs, but I haven't gone so far as to create a system like this and use it as a general sounding board / supporting team for a project. That's quite interesting. What tools have you used to set up these separate personas? How do you keep them up to date with the shared project knowledge?

replies.author: HelfenMich
replies.body:
I started with just an open chat, like you said. As I was initially brainstorming the feasibility of the project, we came up with some ideas and a rough timeline and then I had the idea of adding these AI "team members". I worked with my initial chat to create prompts for the new team members (including a prompt to build what that chat had become). 

Occasionally the context window is full and they start noticeably hallucinating. I use that as an opportunity to spawn a new chat and tweak the old prompt if needed. I also do this thing where I let the "old" chat tweak or add a personality trait in the prompt. It keeps it fresh! 

I'm using Gemini for all of my LLM chats, and I had them generate their own prompts for my team. 

I use GitHub for my git repo and GitHub Issues works well as a kanban board and issue tracker.

I sometimes use a tool called RepoMix that packages up a codebase into a small-ish file meant for LLM consumption. I usually only need to do that for my architect before we refine a new epic or when I need a second opinion.

For basic project documentation, I don't have a perfect solution yet, I'm storing it all in Google Drive and giving access when it updates. "Documentation" in general is an ongoing struggle but something I'm finally starting to prioritize better.

replies.author: interestingsystems
replies.body: That's really quite cool. I think I may borrow some of your ideas here, if you don't mind. Thank you :)

replies.author: HelfenMich
replies.body: Absolutely! I'm always excited to share this with anyone, I'd be happy to help you with my ideas. Feel free to let me know if you come up with anything else that's working great for you, too!

comments.author: Pretend-Park6473
comments.body: Looks radical! Any chance of it running locally?

replies.author: interestingsystems
replies.body: Thank you. Unfortunately, not a chance of running it locally for now. Too much content has to be generated in very little time.

comments.author: icekiller333
comments.body: I love the idea of games that generate art as you play. Great way to argue against people that think art should never be generated - a game that would be impossible without generative art :)

replies.author: interestingsystems
replies.body: Yeah, it definitely wouldn't work any other way :)

comments.author: squirtinagain
comments.body: You should just let people bring their own keys. Pick a handful of models that work well, then let the player pay for the tokens themselves. This solves a few of your problems.

replies.author: interestingsystems
replies.body: Which problems do you feel it solves? The generation costs must still be paid for.

comments.author: Cold-Waltz-5599
comments.body:
I really like this concept of having procedural objects but with generated art that matches it. Art takes a long time to create manually so by automating this step game content and replayability skyrockets, its perfect for rpg's.

So will it be a subscription based game? I can't think of any indie subscription based single-player games. There will need to be a lot of security measures involved so that players cannot abuse the generation tools unless theyre paying for it all. 

Its a cool idea but highly ambitious for indie devs. I am actually doing something very similar but I dont plan to release it publically its just a fun personal project. I do have an idea to do a seasonal thing where it pre-generates a limited amount of characters (im talking couple thousands here :D) so its fresh each run while making the costs fit to a buy once model.

replies.author: interestingsystems
replies.body:
For now I have a credit usage system set up, but I might add a subscription system as well.

I wish you luck with your project, it sounds interesting too. If you can design the game so that it works purely with static content than generating a big batch at regular intervals (or generating downloadable content packs), is a nice way to keep it fresh.
